$comment: Per-family placement rules. Every number here was measured off the STLs
with packages/indexer/src/stl.ts — see packages/indexer/test/families.test.ts,
which re-derives them from the meshes on every run.
Schema 2 introduces archetypes. Wall Control parts share one mounting
interface by construction: seven of the eight sidepiece families have
identical tang, thickness and height geometry, and differ only in how far
they project. Saying that once is both less to get wrong and a truer
description of the system than seventeen near-identical blocks.
A family may omit a size formula. The indexer measures every part anyway,
so a formula here is an assertion that catches bad data, not an input to
placement. Where a family has no single rule, saying nothing is honest.

wallAxes.x: along the wall, increasing to the right
wallAxes.y: depth into the wall, as the design doc has it. The panel's front face is y = 0, so mounted parts occupy y < 0 and anything reaching behind the panel is y > 0.

conventions.printAxes: whatever SketchUp exported. Each archetype declares its own mapping.
conventions.printToWall: wall axis = signed print axis, e.g. y: "+x" means wallY = printX. Every mapping is a proper rotation (determinant +1); mirrored variants ship as separate meshes.
conventions.recentre: STL origins are arbitrary. Translate by -bbox.min before applying any rule.
conventions.depthDatum: Front-flush at the mounting interface. A sidepiece's front face is -(its own depth - tang.depthMm), so a bracket that projects 67 mm sits further out than a flat that projects 18.7 mm. A centerpiece uses the interface depth itself, which is what lands its tab in the socket.

$comment: A sidepiece carries two sockets, not one, and they take the same
centerpiece in two different orientations.
The back plate's socket runs vertically and holds a centerpiece flat
against the panel. The arm's socket runs horizontally, out along the
projection, and holds the same centerpiece as a shelf. Every
shelf-capable centerpiece already has the feature that fits it: a band
repeating every 25.4 mm along the edge, one per grid unit. Ribbed
families fill the pocket with the rib itself; pinned families cut a
matching notch and a 4x10x8 mm pin bridges the two recesses, 4 mm into
each. That is what the pin's odd dimensions are for.
This lives here rather than under either archetype because it is the
interface between them, and the merge in assembly.ts is one level deep,
so a centerpiece family cannot see the sidepiece archetype's blocks.
Measured across all 228 sidepieces. 156 have an arm socket; the 72 that
do not are the Flats (no arm to put one on), the Retainers (a
centerpiece filed under Sidepieces) and the Strap mounts.
armSocket.toleranceNote: Every one of the 156 measures 10.00 long on a 25.40 pitch to within 0.05, which is the resolution of the scan rather than a spread in the models.
armSocket.pocketFloorNote: The floor of the topmost pocket, as a drop from the top of the sidepiece. True of 99 of the 156 - every standard bracket. The rest are the Inverted variants, which put their arm at the bottom (54.85), and the Midmount ones, which put it in the middle (29.45 / 31.10). The planner cannot use those: it never knows which sidepiece holds a given centerpiece, so it has one number to draw with and this is the one that is right for a standard bracket.
armSocket.firstPocketNote: Where pocket 1 begins, measured along the depth axis from the tang end. True of 123 of the 156; the others start a lattice step further out. A shelf's own first band sits bandFirstOffsetMm in from its back edge, so the two together are what set how far the back edge stands off the panel - and why a shelf cannot be drawn flush against it.
armSocket.sidepieceTopNote: A sidepiece's top is always this far above the centre of its topmost engaged slot: h=1 gives 34.9 - 14.55, h=2 gives 57.2 - 36.85, h=3 gives 85.7 - 14.55 - 50.8. Same number every time, which is what lets a shelf be located without knowing the height of whatever holds it.
armSocket.pocketsPerBracketNote: A bracket has exactly one pocket per inch of projection, so a shelf h units deep needs a sidepiece beside it that reaches at least that far. Nothing enforces it here; issues.ts warns.

unsupported.reason: Made for a horizontal Wall Control panel, where the slots run the other way. These locate on the 1/4 inch pegboard holes rather than the vertical slots, so the planner cannot position them meaningfully. They stay in the catalog so you can still find and download them.
unsupported.matchNote: Matched on the part name, case-insensitively, not on the folder. Fourteen of these live in Centerpieces/Locking_spacer_for_horizontal_Wall_Control, but five more are Locking Retainers filed under Sidepieces/Retainers - flagging the folder alone would have missed them.

4x10x8mm Pin.note: Joins a tabless centerpiece to its sidepieces.

8mm Lock Pin.note: Locks a retainer or locking spacer in place.

Quickhook Retainer.note: Press-fits into a Quickhook body. Every hook needs one; the repo's own Quickhooks/README.md says so.

sidepiece.$comment: Verified identical across Flats, Angle brackets, L brackets, Square brackets, U brackets, Strap mounts and Dowel rod hangers: same height series, same 13.7/27.6 thickness, same tang at the same end.
sidepiece.printToWallNote: Left and Right are mirror images in the print depth axis: Left carries its 2.2 mm tang at min.x, Right at max.x. These maps are not free choices - fixing the tang behind the wall, the part upright, and the determinant at +1 leaves no freedom in the third axis. Getting the direction of Y wrong swaps Left and Right while every validity check still passes, which is exactly what the Phase 1 spike check caught.

anchor.bottomBelowSlotCenterNote: Places the tang band centred in its 25.4 mm slot. The odd/even difference is 22.3 mm, the same alternation that generates the height series - two independent derivations agreeing.

depth.note: Front face = -(measured depth - tang.depthMm). Depth is per family and, for U brackets, per part, so it is taken from the mesh rather than declared.

sockets.countNote: Keyed off the Center token: a Center sidepiece is 27.6 mm thick against 13.7 and takes a centerpiece on both faces.

centerpiece.$comment: Height is 25.4h - 0.2 in every centerpiece family that has a rule at all. Families differ in width formula, thickness, and whether they carry tabs.
printToWallNote: A 180 degree turn about wall Z from the map this family shipped with,
which had every centerpiece facing into the panel rather than out of
it. About Z rather than about X on purpose: both turns swap front for
back, but only Z leaves up pointing up, so a hook still opens upward.
The five spacer plates are unchanged by the difference - they are
two-fold symmetric face-on, so the two turns land them identically -
but a hook is not, and one of the two would print the library upside
down.

anchor.bottomBelowSlotCenterNote: Derived from the sidepiece anchor plus the measured 6.6 mm top gap, then checked to be independent of h.

depth.note: = -(18.7 - 8.5): the depth of the mounting interface itself, not of whatever sidepiece happens to hold it. This is what seats the tab in the socket.
socketCentreNote: The middle of the vertical socket groove, in wall Y. Measured off
the Flats: the groove runs -8.30 to -4.10 once a Flat is placed by
its own rule, and every sidepiece cuts the same interface.
This is what a tabbed centerpiece is located by. The part's ear is
measured off its own mesh and put here; the rest of the part
follows. Locating by a face instead only worked while the ear's
offset within the plate stayed put, and it did not.
checks this number, so it cannot drift from the meshes.
plateThicknessNote: The mounting plate, and the reason the anchor above can be written
as a front face at all: a spacer is nothing but the plate, so its
two faces are these 6.15 mm apart and either one would do.
The tab sits 0.5 mm in from the plate's back face in every tabbed
family measured - blank, perforated, locking, U hook, honeycomb and
the tool hooks - so the back face is what the socket actually
locates, at -4.05. A part that carries something adds it in front of
that plate, never behind it, and how much is measured per part.

families.label: Angle bracket
families.sizeNote: The Mid-span Support variants come out 0.16 mm narrower than the rest of their size, hence the loosened tolerance.

families.label: L bracket
families.sizeNote: Some Center variants measure 13.7 rather than 27.6 thick; thickness is taken from the mesh, so this does not affect placement.

families.label: U bracket
families.sizeNote: Depth follows the fractional width in the filename (2.25, 2.5, 3.25, 4.25) rather than a whole number of columns, so no single formula is declared. The indexer measures each part.

families.label: Strap mount
families.sizeNote: All are w=0; depth varies with the strap width named in the file (20/25/30/35 mm), so it is measured rather than derived.

families.label: Retainer
families.shelfNote: Ribbed on one edge only, so as a shelf it is a tongue cantilevered off a single sidepiece rather than a plate spanning two. That is a real way to use one and the lattice fits, but the lock pin does not survive the turn - see the fastener rule.
families.archetypeNote: Filed under Sidepieces but it is not one: it has no tang, and its height follows the centerpiece rule 25.4h - 0.2 rather than the Flats series. It clips onto an assembly, so it takes the centerpiece archetype.

fastenerRules.note: Sidepieces/README.md: a standard retainer just holds the sidepiece against the board and needs nothing. Only the wider locking retainers take the 8 mm lock pin - and only mounted flat, because the pin passes through the plate into the panel and a horizontal plate points it at the ceiling.

families.label: Spacer blank
families.shelfNote: Upstream calls this one a “great choice for horizontal use as a shelf”, and the geometry agrees: the same ribs that sit in the back plate's vertical groove sit in the arm's pockets when the plate is turned.

families.label: Spacer perforated
families.shelfNote: The same plate as Spacer blank with holes in it, and the same rib lattice, so it turns the same way.

families.label: Spacer clip-on
families.shelfNote: Pinned, like Spacer blank flush, and measuring the same notch lattice to within 0.05.

tabs.note: Narrower than its column span rather than wider, so it clears the slot columns instead of reaching into them. No tabs is exactly why this family needs pins.

families.label: Spacer blank flush
families.shelfNote: Pinned rather than ribbed, and upstream calls it “another good choice for horizontal use as a shelf”. Where a ribbed family fills the arm pocket with its own rib, this one cuts a matching 10.0 mm notch and a 4x10x8 mm pin bridges the two recesses, 4 mm into each. Same lattice, 7.60 rather than 7.75 because a pin fills its notch exactly where a 9.8 mm rib leaves 0.1 a side. The notch sits 2.35 into the plate's thickness rather than flush with its face, which is the whole of why bandFloorMm exists.

knownDeviations.note: Measures four columns wide, not five. Either the name or the model is wrong upstream; the indexer places it on its measured width, so it sits correctly but its name overstates it.

families.label: Locking spacer
families.shelfNote: Same rib lattice as the blank. What does not survive the turn is the lock pin - see fastenersByOrientation.
families.sizeNote: Widths span 1-14 columns and do not fit one formula; measured per part.
families.fastenersNote: Centerpieces/Locking_spacer/README.md describes an array of threaded holes and one positive-lock pin screwed into any of them. One is the minimum that locks the part; using more is the owner's choice, so one is what the print list claims.
families.fastenersByOrientationNote: The threaded holes run through the plate, perpendicular to it, so the pin passes through the part and into a 1/4 inch hole in the panel. Mounted flat the plate is parallel to the panel and the pin reaches it. Turned into a shelf the plate is horizontal and the pin points at the ceiling, so there is nothing to lock to and nothing to print.

families.printToWallNote: The identity map, which is the archetype's old map turned a quarter turn out of the wall - the same map the tool hooks and Gridfinity take, and for the same reason. See orientationsNote.
families.label: U hook
families.orientationsNote: Centerpieces/README.md: "U hooks useful for mounting horizontally between side pieces to hang tools." Horizontally, in as many words - a U laid against the panel is a hole, and a U lying flat is a cradle. Third family with no flat orientation, after Gridfinity and the tool hooks.
families.shelfNote: The shared lattice, measured: the ribs sit at 8.2-17.0, 33.6-42.4 and 59.0-67.8 on a 3-unit part, which is the 25.4 pitch every other seating family declares.
families.sizeNote: Thickness is 6.15 for the plate and up to 9.32 where the hook projects; measured per part.

families.label: Gridfinity frame
families.sizeNote: The trailing 1x6 in a name is the Gridfinity grid, not a wall dimension. The five 14-column frames measure 360.0 rather than 361.0, hence the loosened tolerance.
families.printToWallNote: The one family that does not take the centerpiece archetype's map, and the only one rotated a quarter turn out of the wall. Gridfinity is a horizontal system: a frame mounts as a shelf with its cells facing up, so bins stand in it the way they stand on a bench. The archetype map would lay it flat against the panel with the cells facing the room, which is what this planner drew until it was corrected. Sizes still read height x width off the filename; under this map that height becomes how far the shelf projects, which is why depth is measured rather than declared.
families.matesByHeightNote: A shelf does not have to match the height of the sidepiece beside it, because its wall-space height is its 10.8 mm thickness rather than 25.4h - 0.2. Comparing h to a neighbour's h would warn about the wrong thing in both directions.
families.orientationsNote: The only family with no flat orientation at all. Gridfinity is a horizontal system; a frame laid against the panel with its cells facing the room is not a thing anyone builds.
families.shelfNote: Located by its rib, not by its top and not by its bottom. A centerpiece lying in the wall plane is located by its bottom because it fills the socket and 25.4h - 0.2 does the rest; a shelf is 10.8 mm thick whatever its h says, so that anchor drops it clear of the socket. What actually holds it is the rib, in the arm pocket, so that is what the planner lines up: bandFloorMm is where the rib starts within the part's own thickness (0.00 here - the rib is flush with the face it sits on) and bandFirstOffsetMm is how far the first band is in from the back edge. Both measured; both re-derived by the indexer test. Everything else follows from armSocket above.
families.shelfCorrection: This replaces a rule that anchored the frame's top 6.6 mm below the sidepiece top and stood its back edge flush with the panel. Both were wrong, and by the same mistake: 6.6 is the edge of the *back plate's* vertical socket, checked against a tab at 39.8..43.6 in the height axis. A shelf's rib is horizontal and cannot enter a 3.8 mm-deep vertical slot - it belongs in the arm pocket, whose floor is 12.9 below the top and whose first pocket starts 24.05 out from the tang. Seating it properly moves the frame 4.5 mm up and 7.8 mm out.
families.shelfDepthNote: Depth is the filename's height dimension once rotated - 50.6, 101.4, 126.8 or 177.6 mm - so it comes from the mesh rather than the archetype's single constant. Where the back edge lands is not free: the first pocket is 24.05 out from the tang and the first band is 7.75 in from the edge, so the back edge stands 7.8 mm proud of the panel and nothing can push it flush.

printToWallNote: Back to the map the centerpiece archetype used to carry, because this
family carries something. Every centerpiece has the same 2.80 mm tab
ear 0.5 mm in from its plate's back face - measured, spacers and hooks
alike - so the plate is the back 6.15 mm and whatever the part holds
is the rest, in front of it. Turning the archetype puts that rack
behind the ear and therefore inside the panel, which is what
families.test.ts means by 'nothing behind the panel'.
A family that is nothing but the plate has no such stake and takes the
archetype's turn. That is the whole difference.
families.label: Honeycomb storage wall
Quickhook
families.dimensionlessNote: Named by strength and length rather than grid units - `Quickhook 2in Medium`, not `2x0`. They carry no h or w, so they appear in the catalog without facet values, and this family lists its fasteners by name instead of inferring them from a failed dimension parse.
families.printToWallNote: The tang sits at print max.x and print z-min, which is the Flats Right arrangement exactly.
families.sizeNote: Depth is 13.0 + 25.4 x the inches in the name, so a 1in hook is 38.4 deep and projects about 28.4 mm in front of the panel - roughly the inch it advertises, once the 10 mm behind the wall is taken off.

anchor.bottomBelowSlotCenterNote: The 2.2 mm rear plate measures 34.9 mm tall - exactly a 1x0 Flat - and starts 3.0 mm above the bottom of the body. So a Quickhook hangs like a one-unit Flat (14.55) with 3.0 mm of body below it. There is no odd/even alternation because a Quickhook is always one unit.

sockets.countNote: A Quickhook takes no centerpiece. It is a hook, not a side.

families.fastenersNote: Two-part by design: the retainer press-fits into the hook body. The Lockable Retainer and Lock Peg are an alternative locking pair rather than an addition, so they are not counted here.

printToWallNote: The identity map, and not a coincidence: it is exactly the archetype's
old map turned a quarter turn out of the wall, the same move Gridfinity
makes. A tool hook is a tray, not a plaque - a hammer hook holds a
hammer because the handle drops through the arch and the head rests on
top, and a box wrench holder holds wrenches the same way. Laid against
the panel the arch is a hole with nothing under it.
Shipping the asset already turned is what `orientations: ["shelf"]`
means to the indexer, so this map has to bake the shelf pose rather
than the flat one.
The ear does not decide this. Every centerpiece carries the same
2.80 mm ear 0.5 mm in from its plate - spacers and hooks alike - and
armSocket above says why: a sidepiece has two sockets and the same ear
serves the vertical groove flat and the arm pocket turned. It says a
part mounts between two sidepieces, not which way up.
families.label: Tool hook
families.orientationsNote: No flat orientation, for the same reason Gridfinity has none: a tray laid flat against the panel holds nothing. This is the second family to say so.
families.shelfProbeNote: Which part families.test.ts re-derives the lattice from. It reads solidity at the very edge, and most of this family's racks run the full width of their plate, which reads solid the whole way up and hides the bands. The chisel rack is narrower than its plate, so its three ribs are visible where every other part's are not - they are all the same ribs.
shelfNote: The shared lattice, not a per-part measurement: every tool hook whose
rack is narrower than its plate measures 7.70 in from the back edge,
the same number Spacer blank, Locking spacer and Gridfinity declare.
The parts that measure otherwise are the ones whose rack runs the full
width, where a bounding measurement catches the rack rather than the
rib - which is the same reason this family carries `perPart` at all.
bandFloorMm is 0.00 because the ear chamfers out to the face it sits
on, so the rib starts flush.
families.perPartNote: 141 community contributions with no single rule. Height matches 25.4h - 0.2 for 96 of 140 and width matches a known formula for 91 of 140; the rest are neither, because a bounding box here includes the tool-holding geometry rather than just the mounting plate, and several names disagree with their model. Every part is still indexed and placeable - placement comes from the measured mesh - but the vertical anchor is approximate for this family. See Open questions.
